UI and UE are read as one syllable: fui = “fwee”, fue = “fweh”. No written accent, but the stress falls on the second vowel.
Irregular verbs do NOT have a stressed final syllable: hice, tuve, pude (EE-the, TOO-beh), not “hicé”. Unlike the regular ones (hablé)!
1. SER and IR: the same forms!
Surprise: in the indefinido, SER (to be) and IR (to go) have EXACTLY the same forms. The context tells you which is which.
I went to Bucharest. (IR: it has “a” + a place)
The trip was long. (SER: a description)
If “fui” is followed by “a” + a place, it’s IR. If it’s followed by an adjective or a description, it’s SER.
2. The “U” group: tuve, estuve, pude, puse
Most irregulars have a new stem and the same special endings: -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. No accents!
Remember the stem, and the endings are always the same: tuv-e, tuv-iste, tuv-o, tuv-imos, tuv-isteis, tuv-ieron.
Watch the spelling: él HIZO (with a z, not “hico”). And with the J verbs, “ellos” loses the i: dijeron, trajeron (not “dijieron”).
And two short, very common verbs: DAR (to give) → di, diste, dio, dimos, disteis, dieron. VER (to see) → vi, viste, vio, vimos, visteis, vieron.
4. Vowel-changing verbs (only in él and ellos)
-IR verbs that change their vowel in the present also change it in the indefinido, but only in the 3rd person: e → i, o → u.
The same: repetir → repitió, preferir → prefirió, morir → murió.
5. How to talk about a holiday
I went to… / I was in…
Fui en avión / en tren / en coche.
I went by plane / train / car.
The weather was nice / It was very cold.
I had a great time / It was awful.
“Tuve que + infinitive” = “I had to”: Tuve que comprar botas. It’s the past of “tengo que” from chapter 12.
I spent two days in Bucharest.
Pablo and Elena wanted a perfect holiday in Mallorca. It didn’t quite work out.
Last August, Elena and I went to Mallorca with the children.
It all started badly at the airport: the plane left three hours late.
When we arrived, my suitcase didn’t. The airline had lost it.
I had to buy new clothes: two T-shirts, a swimsuit and some sandals.
The hotel wasn’t like in the photos. The room was small and dark.
We asked for another room, but they couldn’t change it.
The next day, Leo ate too much ice cream and was ill all night.
Nobody slept. Elena said: “I want to go home!”
But on the third day everything changed. It was gloriously sunny.
We went to a gorgeous beach, and the children built sandcastles.
In the evening we ate fish at the harbour and looked at the stars.
And on the last day… my suitcase arrived! In the end, we had a great time.

When Grandma Rosario saw the wedding photo, she started telling them about their honeymoon.
“Antonio and I got married on a Saturday in June 1964. It was a wonderful day, but it was terribly hot.”
“We didn’t have much money for the trip, so we went to Santander by train. The journey took twelve hours.”
“When we arrived, we had the first problem: the hotel didn’t have our booking. Antonio was furious.”
“But the owner was very kind. He gave us the best room, with a sea view, for the same price.”
“We stayed there for a week. In the mornings we went to the beach, and in the afternoons we strolled around the harbour.”
“One day Antonio wanted to go fishing. He spent five hours in the boat and caught nothing.”
“In the end he bought two fish at the market and told me he had caught them himself. I realised straight away, of course!”
Everyone laughed. Lucía asked: “And what else did you do, Grandma?”.
“We went to a dance in the town square. Antonio never knew how to dance in his whole life, but that night he danced with me until three.”
“On the last day his parents came to visit us and brought us a present: a wall clock. It still works.”
Grandma pointed to the clock in the living room. They all looked at it in silence.
“That clock has seen our whole life,” she said. “Fifty happy years.”
That evening Lucía wrote in her diary: “Today I discovered that my grandparents were young once too. And that Grandpa was a very bad liar about fish.”
The next morning she asked Grandma to teach her to dance like in 1964. Rosario happily agreed.
